definition: Eschew means to deliberately avoid a thing, habit, or practice on principle.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word eschew. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know eschew should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The columnist eschews exclamation points, arguing that a sentence should earn its emphasis.
Avoid is milder — you might avoid the highway at rush hour with no principle behind it at all; to eschew something is to rule it out always, on principle.
Shun goes further than eschew: it adds cold contempt, usually aims at a person, and refuses all contact.

To forgo is to do without something pleasant or advantageous, often just this once — you forgo dessert, a bonus, a day off. Eschew is sterner and standing: a settled policy of avoiding a practice on principle, every time, not a single sacrifice made in passing.

To spurn is to reject something offered — an invitation, an advance, a deal — with open scorn, in the moment. Eschew is cooler and quieter: a standing habit of avoidance kept on principle, with no drama at all. You spurn one offer loudly; you eschew a practice for a lifetime.

Eschew is a whole-word borrowing: Old French eschiver came from the same old Germanic family that gave us shy, but the connection wore invisible centuries ago, and no modern English word shares a recognizable piece of it. The word survives alone — a formal, slightly old-fashioned way to say you have sworn something off.
Eschew means to deliberately avoid a thing, habit, or practice on principle.
Their grandmother eschews the elevator, taking the four flights to her apartment at her own steady pace, rain or shine.

Eschew is more pointed than avoid because it names a standing, deliberate policy — she is not afraid of the elevator and does not merely miss it now and then; she has ruled it out, on principle, every time.
Eschew is formal and bookish, best for named practices and things — a chef eschews shortcuts, a writer eschews jargon.
It is a quiet standing policy, not a one-time act: abjure, taught in this unit, renounces something once, formally and in public, while shun turns cold contempt on a person.
For everyday talk, plain 'avoid' or 'steer clear of' is the natural choice.

Visitors to Amara Osei's workshop notice the silence first: no whine of routers, no scream of table saws.
Osei eschews power tools entirely, a decision she made at nineteen and has held for thirty years.
It is not nostalgia, she insists, and not fear.
Hand tools force her to feel the grain resist, and furniture built at that pace, she argues, is furniture built to last.
Apprentices who join her sign an agreement: for the length of their training, the machines stay unplugged.
Collectors sometimes ask what she would build with a modern shop at her disposal.
'The same pieces,' she says, 'only worse.'
